title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: reversing words, folding phrases, weighing arguments

questions.prompt: Your module builds "illegal" on legal, "irregular" on regular and "immoral" on moral. A pupil applies the same reasoning to "successful" and writes "insuccessful". Why is that wrong?

options.text: Because in- is only written before a word beginning with a vowel.
Because successful takes un-, a prefix that follows no letter rule.
Because in English only verbs, and never adjectives, take a negative prefix.
Because the negative of successful is built with dis- instead.

questions.explanation: The pupil's reasoning is half right: il-, im-, ir- and in- really are one prefix whose spelling follows the first letter of its word. What that rule cannot tell her is which words take the prefix at all, and successful is not one of them: English reverses it with un-, as it reverses known, wanted, ethical and acceptable. The answer that limits in- to words beginning with a vowel reads too much into inactive and inestimable, since incurable and inhuman both begin with a consonant. The answer that reserves negative prefixes for verbs is contradicted by the module's own list, where legal, moral, regular and curable are all adjectives. The answer that reaches for dis- simply replaces one wrong prefix with another, because dissuccessful is not a word either.

questions.prompt: An insect carries a virus from one field to the next. Two pupils name it: one writes "a virus-carrying insect", the other "a virus-carried insect". Which comment is right?

options.text: The first is right: the insect carries the virus, so the block takes the -ing form.
The second is right: the insect is carried by the virus, so the block takes the past participle.
Both are right, because the two forms mean the same inside a compound adjective.
Neither is right, because the two words of a compound adjective are never joined by a hyphen.

questions.explanation: The test is always who does the action. The insect is the one that carries, so the block takes the -ing form, exactly as your book turns cells that produce insulin into insulin-producing cells. "The second is right: the insect is carried by the virus, so the block takes the past participle." describes the world upside down; the past participle is the form of man-made chemicals, where the chemicals are the ones acted upon. "Both are right, because the two forms mean the same inside a compound adjective." would leave a reader unable to tell which of the two things is doing the carrying. "Neither is right, because the two words of a compound adjective are never joined by a hyphen." contradicts every example in the module, from long-term threat to genetically-modified pea.

questions.prompt: The second speaker of the listening section argues against applying genetic engineering to human beings. Which of these arguments belongs to her list rather than to her opponent's?

options.text: The treatment aims only at the diseased cells and spares the healthy tissue.
A woman whose cancer had already spread to major organs saw her tumours almost disappear after a genetically-engineered drug.
DNA testing can tell people things about themselves they never wanted to know.
Recombinant DNA can free a prisoner convicted of a crime he did not commit.

questions.explanation: The speaker who is against the technique lists its unwanted consequences, and one of them is that DNA testing reveals to people who wish to hide their identity things they never asked to learn: "DNA testing can tell people things about themselves they never wanted to know." The three others are the first speaker's arguments in favour. "The treatment aims only at the diseased cells and spares the healthy tissue." is his case for gene therapy against cancer, set beside the damage that radiation and chemical therapies do. "A woman whose cancer had already spread to major organs was cured by a genetically-engineered drug." is the example he uses to make that case concrete. "Recombinant DNA can free a prisoner convicted of a crime he did not commit." is his fourth point, the one about establishing guilt and innocence. Knowing both lists, and not confusing them, is what the module asks of you; which of the two convinces you is your own business.

questions.prompt: Read this note from a science page. "A hospital in Sfax has tested a small patch that reads the level of sugar through the skin. 90 diabetic patients wore it for three months. In 84 cases the patch gave the same figures as the usual blood test. The hospital has not yet said what the patch will cost." One of these statements is neither confirmed nor denied by the note. Which one?

options.text: The patch was tested on 90 patients.
The patch agreed with the usual blood test in every case.
The trial lasted three months.
The patch is cheaper than the usual blood test.

questions.explanation: The note ends by saying that the price has not been announced, so nothing in it lets you compare the two costs: "The patch is cheaper than the usual blood test." is not mentioned, and a statement you may believe to be true in life is still not mentioned when the text is silent about it. "The patch was tested on 90 patients." is stated word for word, so it is true. "The trial lasted three months." is stated too. "The patch agreed with the usual blood test in every case." is the one the note contradicts: 84 agreements out of 90 leave six that did not agree, so that statement is false, not unmentioned — and telling false apart from not mentioned is the whole point of the exercise.

questions.prompt: A class must write a text whose purpose is to persuade readers to give money for a child's treatment. Which of these openings does the job the genre asks for?

options.text: Renal failure is a condition in which the kidneys stop filtering the blood properly.
Every dinar you send today buys one more week of treatment for a child who has none.
The hospital opened in 1974 and today it has three wards, two laboratories and a garden.
This article will set out the main causes of kidney disease among Tunisian children.

questions.explanation: A text that persuades speaks straight to its reader and asks for something, and "Every dinar you send today buys one more week of treatment for a child who has none." does both: it says you, and it turns the gift into a result the reader can picture. "Renal failure is a condition in which the kidneys stop filtering the blood properly." defines a disease, which belongs to a text whose purpose is to inform. "This article will set out the main causes of kidney disease among Tunisian children." announces an explanation and asks for nothing. "The hospital opened in 1974 and today it has three wards, two laboratories and a garden." describes a building; the reader closes the page with a picture and no reason to act.

questions.prompt: A science page writes: "The largest study yet has dismissed the idea that these devices trigger the illness, but its authors refuse to rule out a risk that only 30 years of use could reveal." What does the sentence say about the risk?

options.text: The study has proved that there is no risk at all.
The study has proved that these devices trigger the illness.
The study has excluded every risk that 30 years of use could reveal.
The study has rejected one fear but has not excluded every risk.

questions.explanation: In a science page dismiss means reject and rule out means exclude, so the sentence rejects one particular fear and then says in so many words that the authors refuse to exclude another: "The study has rejected one fear but has not excluded every risk." "The study has excluded every risk that 30 years of use could reveal." says the opposite of refuse to rule out and is the trap the two verbs are there to set. "The study has proved that there is no risk at all." turns dismissing one idea into proving a general safety, and a study that refuses to exclude a long-term risk has proved nothing of the sort. "The study has proved that these devices trigger the illness." reverses the first half of the sentence entirely, since trigger means activate and that is precisely the idea the study rejected.
